non-biodegradable; hence, they persist in the environment for long periods, reach the food chain and end up accumulating in
the fatty tissue of living organisms. Due to the high persistence and bioaccumulation potential of these chemicals, the Stockholm
Convention classiﬁed most of them as environmental hazards and banned their use. OCP are structurally divided into 4 groups
(Fig. 2): chlorinated derivatives of ethane (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane eDDTe, methoxychlor), chlorinated derivatives of
benzene and cyclohexane (hexachlorobenzene –HCB–, a-, b- and g-hexachlorocyclohexane –HCH– isomers, the latter also known
as lindane), cyclodienes (endosulfan, aldrin, dieldrin, endrin) and chlorinated camphenes (toxaphene and chlordecone). None of
these are currently authorized for use in agriculture in the EU.
OCP are efﬁciently absorbed by respiratory and digestive routes and can easily penetrate through intact skin due to their high
lipophilicity (except for DDT). The biotransformation of DDT is extremely slow and consists of a reductive dehalogenation with
formation of DDE (dichlorodiphenyldichloroethylene), which has a longer half-life. Therefore, the presence of DDE in the blood
indicates long-term exposure, while that of DDT, recent exposure. The high lipophilicity of OCP determines that, once they enter the
